title: Dental Procedure Costs With & Without Insurance: Braces, Crowns, and Fillings
description: What braces, crowns, and fillings actually cost with and without dental insurance, plus whether you can legally carry two dental plans at once — answered question by question.
author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: Braces without insurance typically run $3,000-$7,000 for traditional metal braces and $4,000-$8,000+ for Invisalign, while a crown without insurance usually falls between $1,000 and $2,500 depending on the material and whether it's placed on a front or back tooth.

Most dental PPO plans cover fillings under "basic services" at 70-80% co-insurance after the deductible, meaning a patient typically pays $30-$80 out of pocket per filling once insurance applies, versus $150-$400 with no coverage at all.

Orthodontic coverage is usually a separate rider with its own lifetime maximum (commonly $1,000-$3,000) that applies once per lifetime per covered person, so it doesn't reset annually the way basic and preventive benefits do.

You can legally hold two dental insurance plans at once, and coordination of benefits (COB) rules — not a blanket doubling of coverage — determine how much of the remaining bill the second plan actually pays.

California's higher regional labor and lab costs generally push orthodontic pricing above national averages, so a Los Angeles or Bay Area quote for braces is a poor proxy for what someone in a lower-cost state would pay for the identical treatment plan.

faqs.question: Does dental insurance cover the full cost of braces?
faqs.answer: No. Orthodontic benefits are typically paid at 50% co-insurance up to a separate lifetime maximum, commonly $1,000 to $3,000, so even a well-insured patient usually still owes several thousand dollars out of pocket for a full course of treatment.

faqs.question: Is it worth getting dental insurance just for a crown or root canal?
faqs.answer: It depends on your plan's waiting period and annual maximum. Many plans impose a 6- to 12-month waiting period before major services like crowns are covered, and annual maximums (often $1,000-$2,000) can be reached quickly by a single major procedure, so run the math on your specific plan's numbers before assuming coverage will offset the full premium cost.

faqs.question: Will having two dental insurance plans mean I pay nothing out of pocket?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Coordination of benefits caps the combined payout from both plans at 100% of the allowed charge, not 200%, so the second plan typically closes some or all of the remaining gap rather than creating a duplicate payment or profit.

content.text: Dental cost searches almost always come from one of two places: someone staring at a treatment estimate trying to figure out whether the number in front of them is normal, or someone trying to decide whether buying (or adding a second) dental plan is even worth it before a big procedure. Below are the specific cost questions people actually search, answered with real dollar ranges and the plan mechanics that explain why the final bill lands where it does.
How Much Does It Cost for Braces Without Insurance?

Without any orthodontic coverage, traditional metal braces typically cost $3,000 to $7,000 for a full course of treatment (usually 18-30 months), with ceramic braces running somewhat higher and [clear aligner systems like Invisalign](/compare/traditional-braces-vs-invisalign) commonly landing at $4,000-$8,000 or more depending on case complexity. The total is driven mainly by treatment length and case severity rather than the type of bracket alone — a straightforward bite correction on a teenager costs meaningfully less than a complex adult case involving jaw alignment or [extractions](/qa/how-much-does-a-tooth-extraction-cost-without-insurance). Many orthodontic offices offer in-house 0%-interest payment plans spread over the treatment period specifically because so many patients pay this bill without insurance — see the [complete braces pricing and payment-plan breakdown](/qa/how-much-does-it-cost-for-braces-without-insurance) for the material-by-material numbers.
How Much Is a Crown Without Insurance?

A single [dental crown without insurance](/qa/how-much-is-a-crown-without-insurance) generally costs $1,000 to $2,500 per tooth, with the exact figure driven by material choice — porcelain-fused-to-metal crowns typically sit at the lower end, all-ceramic or zirconia crowns run higher, and gold crowns (still used on back molars for durability) vary with current metal prices. Front teeth crowns are often priced slightly higher than back-tooth crowns because of the additional cosmetic shading and layering work needed to match adjacent teeth. If a [root canal](/qa/how-much-does-a-root-canal-cost-with-insurance) is required before the crown is placed, that adds a separate $700-$1,500+ depending on the tooth's number of canals, on top of the crown cost itself — and if the tooth can't be saved at all, a [surgical extraction](/qa/how-much-does-a-tooth-extraction-cost-without-insurance) followed by a [bridge or implant](/compare/dental-implant-vs-dental-bridge) becomes the alternative path.

rows: $300 - $750 after deductible (50-70% coinsurance, often a "major service")
$1,500 - $5,500 after 50% orthodontic coinsurance up to lifetime max

content.title: Why the ranges are wide
content.text: *Out-of-pocket figures assume a standard employer PPO plan with a $50-$100 deductible, an annual maximum of $1,000-$2,000, and no waiting period already satisfied. Your actual cost depends heavily on whether you've met your deductible, how much of your annual maximum is already used, and your specific plan's coinsurance tier for that procedure category.
How Much Does Fillings Cost With Insurance?

[Fillings](/qa/how-much-does-fillings-cost-with-insurance) are classified as a "basic service" on most dental PPO plans, which typically pays 70-80% of the allowed amount once your annual deductible (commonly $25-$100) is met — leaving a patient-owed balance of roughly $30-$80 for a standard one- or two-surface filling, versus $150-$400 with no coverage at all. Composite (tooth-colored) fillings on front teeth are sometimes reimbursed at a lower rate than amalgam fillings on some older plan designs, so it's worth confirming your specific plan's coverage for the material your dentist plans to use, particularly on a back molar where amalgam is still common. Basic services like this are a different coverage tier entirely from periodontal treatment — if a cleaning has progressed to a [deep cleaning](/qa/how-much-does-a-deep-cleaning-cost-with-insurance) because of gum disease, expect a noticeably different coinsurance rate than the one that applies to a routine filling.
Can You Have Two Dental Insurance Plans?

Yes — [there's no legal restriction on holding two dental insurance plans](/qa/can-you-have-two-dental-insurance-plans) at the same time, and it's fairly common for a married couple to each be covered under their own employer's plan plus their spouse's as a dependent. What changes is how the bill gets paid: insurers use coordination of benefits (COB) rules to decide which plan pays first (the "primary" plan, typically the one tied to your own employment) and which pays second ("secondary"), rather than each plan independently paying its full share as if the other didn't exist.
How Does Coordination of Benefits Actually Work With Two Plans?

The primary plan processes the claim first and pays its normal share under its own coinsurance and deductible rules. The claim (and the remaining balance) then goes to the secondary plan, which typically pays up to its own coverage percentage of the allowed amount — but the combined payment from both plans is capped at 100% of the total allowed charge, not 200%. In practice this means a second plan is most valuable for closing the specific gap left by the first plan's deductible, coinsurance percentage, or annual maximum, rather than doubling your total reimbursement. For a dependent child covered under both parents' plans, the "birthday rule" is the common COB standard: whichever parent's birthday falls earlier in the calendar year is typically the primary plan. See the [full coordination-of-benefits walkthrough](/qa/can-you-have-two-dental-insurance-plans), including the divorced-parent exception to the birthday rule, for the complete picture.

items: Tell your dentist's office about both plans before treatment so they can bill the correct primary plan first.
Confirm which plan is primary — usually determined by your own employer-sponsored plan taking priority over a spouse's plan, or the birthday rule for dependent children.
Let the primary plan's Explanation of Benefits (EOB) process fully before the secondary plan is billed for the remainder.
Check both plans' combined annual maximum situations separately — a second plan's own annual maximum is a genuinely separate pool, even though COB caps total reimbursement at 100% of the bill.

content.text: How Much Do Braces Cost in California With Insurance?

In California, particularly in higher-cost metro areas like Los Angeles, San Francisco, and San Diego, orthodontic pricing tends to run above the national average due to higher orthodontist overhead, staff wages, and lab fees — a full course of traditional braces frequently lands in the $4,500-$8,000 range before insurance, compared to the $3,000-$7,000 national range cited earlier. With a standard orthodontic rider (typically 50% coinsurance up to a $1,000-$2,500 lifetime maximum), a California patient still commonly owes $3,000-$6,000 out of pocket even with coverage, since the lifetime maximum doesn't scale up for regional cost differences the way the treatment price itself does. Getting a specific written treatment plan and cost estimate from a California-licensed orthodontist — rather than relying on a national average — is the only reliable way to know your actual number. [One San Diego family's real numbers](/scenarios/elena-california-braces-insurance-gap) walk through exactly how this gap plays out when a 50% orthodontic rider meets above-average California pricing.
Why Do Annual and Lifetime Maximums Matter More Than the Coinsurance Percentage?

A plan advertising "80% coverage on basic services" sounds generous, but most dental plans cap total annual payout at $1,000-$2,000 regardless of coinsurance percentage — a figure that hasn't kept pace with dental cost inflation the way medical insurance maximums have, since dental plans were historically designed as a cost-sharing benefit rather than true catastrophic protection. This is also why orthodontic coverage is carved out into its own separate lifetime maximum rather than pulling from the same annual pool as fillings and cleanings — without that separation, one course of braces would exhaust several years of basic-service coverage in a single claim. Before assuming a dental plan will meaningfully offset a large treatment plan like a full mouth of crowns or a complete orthodontic case, check the specific annual and lifetime maximum dollar figures on your plan summary, not just the advertised coinsurance percentage — and confirm your [plan's waiting period](/learn/dental-insurance-waiting-periods-explained) for that service tier has actually been satisfied, since a major-service claim filed too early is one of the most common and entirely avoidable reasons a claim gets denied.
What About Extractions, Implants, Bridges, and Cleanings?

The four procedures above cover most search intent, but they're not the only dental costs people budget for. A [tooth extraction without insurance](/qa/how-much-does-a-tooth-extraction-cost-without-insurance) is often the lower-cost path when a tooth is too damaged to save with a filling or crown — $150-$300 for a simple extraction, or $300-$800+ if it's surgical, which describes most impacted wisdom teeth. [Jake's case study](/scenarios/jake-austin-wisdom-teeth-no-insurance) shows what that actually looks like for a 20-year-old who aged off his parents' plan and had to budget for four impacted wisdom teeth with zero coverage. If a missing tooth needs to be replaced afterward, the choice is usually between a [dental implant](/qa/how-much-does-a-dental-implant-cost-without-insurance) ($3,000-$5,000+, surgical, leaves neighboring teeth untouched) and a [dental bridge](/qa/how-much-does-a-dental-bridge-cost-without-insurance) ($2,000-$5,000, no surgery, but permanently reshapes the two healthy anchor teeth) — see the [full implant-vs-bridge comparison](/compare/dental-implant-vs-dental-bridge) for how insurance treats each differently.

Two other cost questions come up constantly alongside these procedures. If a routine cleaning has progressed into gum disease territory, a [deep cleaning](/qa/how-much-does-a-deep-cleaning-cost-with-insurance) is billed and reimbursed on a completely different tier than the twice-yearly cleaning most plans cover near 100% — expect per-quadrant pricing and standard basic- or major-service coinsurance instead. And on the opposite end of the spectrum, [teeth whitening and veneers](/qa/does-dental-insurance-cover-teeth-whitening-or-veneers) are almost universally excluded from dental insurance altogether, since coverage is built around restoring function, not improving appearance — no coinsurance tier applies to either one, full stop.

content.text: This article is educational and general in nature and does not constitute dental, financial, or insurance advice. Procedure costs and plan reimbursement percentages vary significantly by provider, geographic region, specific plan design, and individual treatment complexity. Confirm exact costs and coverage details with your dentist's billing office and your specific dental plan's summary of benefits before treatment.
